291.event_title: Elisabeth Kubler-Ross talks honestly with dying patients
291.place: University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, United States
291.event: In 1965 the psychiatrist Elisabeth Kubler-Ross joined the University of Chicago and began a series of seminars in which terminally ill patients were interviewed and allowed to speak openly about their illness and their care. At the time many doctors avoided telling patients that their condition was terminal, and some colleagues thought her seminars cruel, but she found that patients wanted to be treated as people and spoken to frankly. Her book On Death and Dying (1969), drawn from these interviews, helped change the medical approach to the care of the dying.
291.explanation: Kubler-Ross showed that honest speech, offered with compassion, relieved the isolation of the dying rather than harming them, and her work helped make truthful, caring conversation part of end-of-life medicine.
291.tie_back: The kural defines truthfulness as speech that brings no harm to anyone, and Kubler-Ross demonstrated that even the hardest truths could be spoken in a way that comforted rather than wounded.
291._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of truth joined to harmlessness, though the kural's claim is a definition of truth itself, which the event only partly dramatises.

292.event_title: Doctors at Rome's Fatebenefratelli Hospital invent K Syndrome
292.place: Fatebenefratelli Hospital, Tiber Island, Rome, Italy
292.event: After the Nazi round-up of Jews in Rome on 16 October 1943, doctors at the Fatebenefratelli Hospital, led by head physician Giovanni Borromeo, admitted Jewish and anti-fascist refugees as patients and listed them in official records as suffering from K Syndrome, an invented and supposedly contagious disease. Occupying soldiers who searched the hospital avoided the wards said to hold these patients, and the hospital continued sheltering refugees until the Allies entered Rome in June 1944. In 2004 Yad Vashem recognised Borromeo as Righteous Among the Nations.
292.explanation: The doctors deliberately told a falsehood whose only purpose and effect was to save innocent lives, at serious risk to themselves.
292.tie_back: The kural says even a falsehood takes the place of truth when it yields good wholly free of fault, and the invented disease that protected refugees is about as clear a case of such a blameless lie as history offers.
292._accuracy_note: Very close to a dramatisation of the kural, since the lie harmed no innocent person and existed only to save lives; estimates of how many were saved vary between sources.

293.event_title: Thomas More refuses to swear the oath his conscience rejected
293.place: Lambeth Palace and the Tower of London, London, England
293.event: On 13 April 1534 Sir Thomas More, the former Lord Chancellor, appeared before the king's commissioners at Lambeth and said he would accept the royal succession but refused to swear the Oath of Succession, whose preamble renounced papal authority and affirmed Henry VIII's supremacy over the Church. He was imprisoned in the Tower of London, where he was interrogated several times and continued to refuse to affirm what he did not believe. He was convicted of treason on 1 July 1535 and beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535.
293.explanation: More chose imprisonment and death rather than state on oath something his own conscience held to be false.
293.tie_back: The kural warns never to lie about what one's own heart knows to be true, and More would not utter such a lie even to save his life.
293._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of refusing to lie against one's own knowledge, though it shows the precept being kept rather than the burning conscience of one who breaks it.

294.event_title: Walter Cronkite is named the most trusted man in America
294.event: Walter Cronkite anchored the CBS Evening News from the early 1960s until 1981 and was known for his adherence to journalistic integrity, reporting events from the Kennedy assassination to the Moon landing. In 1972 an Oliver Quayle poll named him the most trusted man in America, ranking him above the president, the vice-president and members of Congress. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1981.
294.explanation: Cronkite's standing rested on a public belief that he would not knowingly deceive his audience, and that trust gave him lasting affection across a divided country.
294.tie_back: The kural says one who lives without falsehood dwells in the hearts of all people, and Cronkite's reputation for truthfulness won him a place in the regard of a whole nation.
294._accuracy_note: A good fit for truthfulness winning a place in people's hearts, though some media historians question how rigorous the 1972 poll was.

295.event_title: Martin Luther refuses to recant at the Diet of Worms
295.event: Martin Luther, whose Ninety-five Theses of 1517 had condemned the sale of indulgences, was summoned before the Diet of the Holy Roman Empire at Worms under a safe-conduct. On 18 April 1521 he refused to repudiate his writings unless convinced of error by Scripture or by reason, declaring that his conscience was bound by the Word of God. The Edict of Worms then banned his writings and declared him a heretic and outlaw.
295.explanation: Luther's protest began as a challenge to the idea that religious merit could be bought through payments, and at Worms he placed sincere conviction above every outward religious authority.
295.tie_back: The kural ranks truth spoken in harmony with one's heart above both austerity and charity, and Luther, who had attacked purchased indulgences, insisted at Worms that he could speak only what his conscience held true.
295._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the event shows truth from the heart over outward religion, though the comparison with austerity and gift-giving is only implicit.

296.event_title: Raja Harishchandra, the story of the truthful king, opens India's film industry
296.event: Dadasaheb Phalke's silent film Raja Harishchandra, widely regarded as the first full-length Indian feature film, was released at the Coronation Cinema in Bombay on 3 May 1913. It told the legend of King Harishchandra, who gave up his kingdom and family to keep his word to the sage Vishwamitra and was finally restored. Because no women would take the roles, Phalke cast men in the female parts, and the film was a great success; only fragments survive today.
296.explanation: When India's first feature film needed a story that every audience would know and honour, it turned to the legend of a king remembered above all for never breaking faith with the truth.
296.tie_back: The kural says there is no fame like that of never lying, and the enduring fame of the truthful Harishchandra was strong enough to launch an entire national cinema.
296._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the film is a real, documented event, but the truthful figure it celebrates is legendary, and some historians debate its claim to be the very first Indian feature.

297.event_title: Solzhenitsyn publishes Live Not by Lies on the day of his arrest
297.event: On 12 February 1974, the day KGB officers arrested him at his Moscow flat, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn released his essay Live Not by Lies. It urged Soviet citizens not to attempt heroic protest but simply to refuse personal participation in lies, by not writing, signing, saying or voting for anything they did not believe. The next day he was stripped of his Soviet citizenship and deported to West Germany.
297.explanation: Solzhenitsyn argued that an ordinary person who did nothing else but steadfastly refuse to lie could help bring down a system that depended on lies.
297.tie_back: The kural says that if one practises truthfulness without ever failing, it is well even if one does no other virtuous deed, which is almost exactly the programme Solzhenitsyn set out in his essay.
297._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's claim that unfailing non-lying is sufficient in itself, though Solzhenitsyn framed it politically rather than as a complete ethic.

298.event_title: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission
298.event: The Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act of 1995 created South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, to uncover the truth about gross human rights violations committed between 1960 and 1994. Victims gave testimony, and the Commission's Amnesty Committee could grant amnesty for politically motivated acts only to applicants who made full disclosure of the relevant facts. Of 7,112 people who applied, 849 were granted amnesty.
298.explanation: The Commission made full and truthful disclosure, rather than punishment alone, the path by which a divided country sought to cleanse itself of its past.
298.tie_back: The kural says outer cleanliness comes from water but inner purity is seen only through truthfulness, and the Commission tried to purify a nation's conscience by requiring the whole truth to be told.
298._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: amnesty was a legal rather than moral cleansing, and the Commission has been criticised for its narrow scope.

299.event_title: Nehru's broadcast after Gandhi's death: the light that shone was no ordinary light
299.event: On the evening of 30 January 1948, after Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke to the nation over All India Radio without a prepared text. He began by saying that the light had gone out of their lives, then corrected himself, saying that the light that had shone in India was no ordinary light and would still be seen a thousand years later, because it represented the living, eternal truths. He urged his listeners not to respond to the killing with violence.
299.explanation: Nehru described Gandhi's lifelong devotion to truth as a light that death could not put out.
299.tie_back: The kural says ordinary lamps are not true lamps and that for the wise only the lamp of truthfulness is the real lamp, which is the very image Nehru reached for when he spoke of Gandhi.
299._accuracy_note: A strong illustration that uses the kural's own metaphor of truth as an undying light; transcripts of the extempore speech differ slightly in wording.

300.event_title: Truth Prevails becomes the motto on the Czechoslovak and Czech presidential flag
300.event: After Czechoslovakia became independent in 1918, its first president, Tomas Garrigue Masaryk, drew on the heritage of the reformer Jan Hus and placed a version of the Hussite motto Truth Prevails on the presidential flag. When the Czech Republic was established, its law on state symbols retained the words Pravda vitezi (Truth Prevails) on the flag of the president, where they remain.
300.explanation: A modern state chose truth, above power or glory, as the single watchword to fly over its head of state.
300.tie_back: The kural concludes that among all things found to be real, nothing surpasses truthfulness, a verdict a whole nation echoed by making Truth Prevails the motto of its highest office.
300._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the motto affirms the supremacy of truth, though it is a national symbol rather than a personal act of truthfulness.
